atoms.1: Fatigue and dark urine suggest hemolysis (the breakdown of red blood cells).
atoms.2: Recent trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prescription can trigger hemolysis in patients with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency.
atoms.3: Conjunctival icterus (yellowing of the eyes due to elevated bilirubin from hemolysis) is noted on physical exam.
atoms.4: Bilateral flank tenderness possibly indicates hemoglobinuria or renal involvement from hemolysis.
atoms.5: Hemoglobin: 7.2 g/dL is low, indicating anemia from hemolysis.
atoms.6: Total bilirubin: 2.1 mg/dL with indirect bilirubin predominance is elevated, consistent with hemolysis.
atoms.7: Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH): 470 U/L is elevated, a marker of cell turnover and hemolysis.
atoms.8: G6PD levels can be normal during an acute hemolytic episode due to the destruction of older, more enzyme-deficient cells.
atoms.9: Younger cells have relatively higher G6PD activity during an acute hemolytic episode.
atoms.10: Acanthocytes are associated with liver disease or abetalipoproteinemia.
atoms.11: Codocytes (target cells) are seen in thalassemias, liver disease, and hemoglobinopathies.
atoms.12: Degmacytes (bite cells) are formed when macrophages 'bite' out a portion of the red cell containing denatured hemoglobin (Heinz bodies).
atoms.13: Degmacytes (bite cells) are commonly seen in G6PD deficiency.
atoms.14: Schistocytes are fragmented cells seen in microangiopathic hemolytic anemias like DIC, TTP, or HUS.
atoms.15: Spherocytes are seen in hereditary spherocytosis and autoimmune hemolytic anemia.
atoms.16: Given the patient's clinical presentation and the likely diagnosis, the peripheral blood smear will most likely show degmacytes (bite cells).
atoms.17: Oxidative damage caused by the drug leads to the removal of denatured hemoglobin by the spleen.

snippets.output: The patient's symptoms of fatigue and dark urine suggest hemolysis, which can be triggered by trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole in patients with G6PD deficiency. Conjunctival icterus and bilateral flank tenderness may indicate hemoglobinuria or renal involvement from hemolysis.

Laboratory results show hemoglobin at 7.2 g/dL, indicating anemia from hemolysis. Total bilirubin is 2.1 mg/dL with indirect bilirubin predominance, and LDH is 470 U/L, both elevated and consistent with hemolysis.
G6PD levels can be normal during an acute hemolytic episode due to the destruction of older, more enzyme-deficient cells, leaving younger cells with relatively higher G6PD activity.
Degmacytes (bite cells) are formed when macrophages 'bite' out a portion of the red cell containing denatured hemoglobin (Heinz bodies) and are commonly seen in G6PD deficiency.

Acanthocytes are associated with liver disease or abetalipoproteinemia. Codocytes (target cells) are seen in thalassemias, liver disease, and hemoglobinopathies. Schistocytes are seen in microangiopathic hemolytic anemias like DIC, TTP, or HUS. Spherocytes are seen in hereditary spherocytosis and autoimmune hemolytic anemia.

Given the patient's clinical presentation and the likely diagnosis of G6PD deficiency-induced hemolysis, the peripheral blood smear will most likely show degmacytes (bite cells). Oxidative damage caused by the drug leads to the removal of denatured hemoglobin by the spleen.
